questions.question: Compare JWT vs Session-based vs OAuth2 vs SAML authentication — when to use each?
questions.title: Authentication Strategies: JWT vs Session vs OAuth2 vs SAML
questions.direct_answer: **Session auth** stores a random session ID in a cookie; server keeps state (Redis or sticky). Simple, instantly revocable, secure by default. **JWT** stores signed claims in a token carried in headers; stateless, scales horizontally, but **revocation is hard**. **OAuth2** is a **delegation framework** — you redirect to an authorization server (Google, Okta, Auth0, Cognito) which authenticates and returns tokens. **OIDC** sits on OAuth2 for identity. **SAML** is XML-based enterprise SSO — common in B2B/workforce, heavier than OIDC. **2026 rule**: first-party web -> **session + cookies**; APIs/microservices -> **OIDC JWT** (short-lived + refresh); enterprise SSO -> **SAML or OIDC** by IdP; mobile -> **OIDC + PKCE**.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of different auth patterns, trade-offs, and when to pick each
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: 'JWT is stateless so always better'; putting sensitive data in JWT; not knowing revocation challenges
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Discuss short-lived access tokens + refresh, PKCE, token introspection, SAML vs OIDC in enterprise

sections.title: Four Different Things, Often Conflated
sections.content:
These are often conflated but solve different problems.

**Session-based** — user logs in; server generates a random session ID; sets it as `HttpOnly` cookie; stores session state server-side (Redis, DB, in-memory). Every request includes the cookie; server looks up the session. **State lives on the server.**

**JWT (JSON Web Token)** — a token format. Base64-encoded JSON with signature (HS256 or RS256). Claims (`userId`, `role`, `exp`) encoded in the token. Sent in `Authorization: Bearer <token>` header. Server verifies signature; no lookup needed. **State lives in the token.**

**OAuth2** — an **authorization framework**, not authentication per se. Defines flows (Authorization Code, Client Credentials, Device Code) for clients to obtain tokens from an Authorization Server. Common today via **OIDC** (OpenID Connect), which adds ID tokens for authentication.

**SAML 2.0** — XML-based enterprise SSO standard. User logs in once at IdP; IdP issues SAML assertions (signed XML) that SPs consume. Heavy in enterprise (Okta, Azure AD, ADFS, Ping).

**Key distinction:**
- Session/JWT are **token formats** for authenticated requests
- OAuth2/OIDC/SAML are **protocols** for obtaining tokens and delegating identity
- An OAuth2 flow can produce a JWT access token sent with each call
- A session-based web app can be authenticated via SAML SSO

sections.title: Auth Flow Comparison
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart TB
    sUser["Session: User"] -->|login| sApp["App Server"]
    sApp -->|create session| sStore["Redis session store"]
    sApp -->|"Set-Cookie sessionId"| sUser
    sUser -->|cookie| sApp
    sApp -.lookup.-> sStore

    jUser["JWT: User"] -->|login| jApp["App Server"]
    jApp -->|sign token| jUser
    jUser -->|Bearer token| jApp
    jApp -.verify signature.-> jApp

    oUser["OAuth2 OIDC: User"] -->|redirect| oAS["Authorization Server"]
    oAS -->|authenticate| oUser
    oUser -->|auth code| oClient["Client App"]
    oClient -->|code + secret| oAS
    oAS -->|access_token + id_token| oClient
    oClient -->|Bearer access_token| oApi["Resource API"]
    oApi -.validate JWT or introspect.-> oAS

    saUser["SAML: User"] -->|access SP| saSp["Service Provider"]
    saSp -->|redirect| saIdp["Identity Provider"]
    saIdp -->|login + SAML assertion| saUser
    saUser -->|POST assertion| saSp
    saSp -.validate signed XML.-> saSp
```

sections.title: Feature Comparison
sections.content:
| Dimension | Session | JWT | OAuth2 / OIDC | SAML |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Statefulness** | Server state | Stateless | Depends (JWT or opaque) | Typically session after assertion |
| **Revocation** | Instant (delete session) | Hard (need blocklist) | Hard for JWT; easy for opaque | Logout via IdP SLO |
| **Scalability** | Shared session store needed | Horizontal-friendly | Horizontal-friendly | Horizontal-friendly |
| **Storage** | HttpOnly cookie | Authorization header | Both | POST body assertion |
| **Size** | Tiny (session ID) | Can grow with claims | JWT can grow | Large (XML) |
| **Typical use** | Server-rendered web | API auth between services | Third-party identity, SSO | Enterprise SSO |
| **Mobile friendly** | Possible with cookie | Yes (common) | Yes (common) | Clunky |
| **Cross-domain** | Limited by cookie rules | Easy | Easy | Via federation |
| **Standard maturity** | Decades | RFC 7519 (2015) | RFC 6749 (2012); OIDC 2014 | SAML 2.0 (2005) |
| **Implementation effort** | Low | Low | Medium-high | High |
| **Security gotchas** | CSRF (use SameSite) | XSS exposes token; revocation | Redirect attacks; PKCE | XML signature wrapping |
| **Token life** | Minutes to hours | Minutes (access); hours/days (refresh) | Minutes (access); days (refresh) | Hours |
| **Spring module** | spring-session | spring-security-oauth2-resource-server | spring-security-oauth2-client / resource-server | spring-security-saml2-service-provider |

sections.title: Decision Framework
sections.content:
**Pick session-based when:**
- First-party web application; user logs into your site directly
- Server-rendered pages (Thymeleaf, Next.js with session)
- Single domain or subdomain sharing
- Need instant revocation (logout, admin ban)
- Prefer simplicity — no token plumbing
- Redis / shared session store is acceptable infra

**Pick JWT (raw) when:**
- Service-to-service calls between your own services (short-lived tokens signed by trust store)
- Mobile or SPA talking to your own API
- Need stateless scaling across many API instances
- Latency-sensitive — avoid per-request DB/Redis lookup
- Can accept delayed revocation (up to expiry) or implement `jti` blocklist

**Pick OAuth2 / OIDC when:**
- 'Login with Google/Microsoft/GitHub' — using external IdPs
- Enterprise SSO with modern IdP (Okta, Auth0, Cognito, Keycloak)
- Federated identity across multiple apps
- Microservice architecture with central auth server
- Need OAuth2 scopes for fine-grained API authorization
- Mobile apps with **PKCE** (mandatory for public clients)

**Pick SAML when:**
- Enterprise B2B integration (customer mandates SAML for SSO)
- Legacy enterprise systems (banks, government, insurance)
- ADFS, Azure AD SAML (though Azure AD pushes OIDC)
- IdP-initiated flows required

**Real-world patterns:**
- **E-commerce**: session + cookies for user; JWT for service-to-service
- **SaaS B2B**: OIDC for login (customers bring their IdP); JWT for APIs
- **Banking**: session for web; OIDC for mobile; SAML for corporate customers
- **Internal company tools**: SAML SSO to corporate IdP
- **Developer API platform**: OAuth2 with scopes; access + refresh tokens

sections.title: Production Best Practices
sections.content:
**Session best practices:**
- `HttpOnly` (JS can't read), `Secure` (HTTPS only), `SameSite=Lax|Strict` (CSRF)
- Rotate session ID on login (prevent fixation)
- Short idle timeout (15-30min) + sliding renewal
- Redis with TTL for scale
- Optional fingerprinting (IP/UA) — handle mobile IP changes gracefully

**JWT best practices:**
- **Short expiry** (access tokens 15min; refresh days-weeks)
- Sign with **asymmetric keys (RS256/ES256)** for multi-service
- Include `jti` (JWT ID) for revocation tracking
- Validate `iss`, `aud`, `exp`, `nbf`, signature
- Don't put sensitive data in claims (signed, not encrypted)
- Token size: keep <4KB total
- Revocation: Redis blocklist + `jti`, OR opaque + introspection for revocable flows
- HTTPS only; never over HTTP
- Store in `Authorization` header, not `localStorage` (XSS); SPAs: session-cookie + token-in-memory

**OAuth2 / OIDC best practices:**
- **Authorization Code + PKCE** for all clients (public mandatory, confidential recommended)
- Never use Implicit flow (deprecated)
- Don't use Resource Owner Password Credentials (anti-pattern)
- Validate ID token signature, nonce, audience, issuer
- `state` parameter to prevent CSRF on redirect
- Short-lived access tokens; refresh tokens rotatable
- Token introspection for revocation
- Discovery endpoint: `.well-known/openid-configuration`

**SAML best practices:**
- Always sign assertions
- Validate signature with IdP's public cert
- Check `NotBefore`, `NotOnOrAfter`, `Audience`, `Recipient`
- Validate `InResponseTo` matches original request
- Prevent XML signature wrapping (use OpenSAML, Spring Security SAML)
- Single Logout (SLO) if mandated
- Cert rotation plan for IdP rollover

**Common security mistakes:**
- **JWT in `localStorage`** — XSS risk
- **Not validating signature** — trusting the claim
- **Accepting `alg: none`** — famous JWT attack
- **Long-lived access tokens** — revocation impossible
- **No PKCE on mobile/SPA** — auth code interception possible
- **No CSRF on cookie sessions** — use `SameSite` + CSRF token for state changes
- **Trusting JWT issuer without whitelist** — validate `iss`
- **Forgetting `aud` check** — token for service A accepted by service B

**Spring Security sample (Resource Server):**

```java
@Configuration
@EnableWebSecurity
public class Sec {
    @Bean
    SecurityFilterChain chain(HttpSecurity http) throws Exception {
        return http.authorizeHttpRequests(a -> a.anyRequest().authenticated())
            .oauth2ResourceServer(o -> o.jwt(Customizer.withDefaults()))
            .build();
    }
}
```

```yaml
spring.security.oauth2.resourceserver.jwt.issuer-uri: https://login.example.com/
```

For SAML, use `spring-security-saml2-service-provider` with `RelyingPartyRegistration`.

sections.title: Myth-Busting and the Bigger Picture
sections.content:
**When session helps:**
- First-party web — simplest, instantly revocable
- Compliance: instant logout enforceable
- Strong CSRF defense via `SameSite`

**When JWT helps:**
- Microservices where each validates independently
- Mobile/SPA without cookie semantics
- Edge / API-gateway validation without DB hop

**When it hurts:**
- 'JWT is better because stateless' — false for most web apps
- 'Session doesn't scale' — Redis-backed scales fine
- 'JWT needs no DB lookup' — revocation, role changes often need one anyway
- Long-lived JWT without revocation plan -> blast radius is huge

**Watch for:**
- **JWT in `localStorage`** = XSS-readable; use `HttpOnly` cookie or in-memory
- **Session without `SameSite`** = CSRF-vulnerable
- **`alg: none` JWT attack** — libraries should reject; pin allowed algorithms
- **Refresh token rotation** — detects reuse and revokes the family
- **2026 trend: Passkeys (FIDO2/WebAuthn)** — passwordless, layered on top of session/OAuth2
- **Zero-trust** — mTLS service-to-service + per-request short-lived tokens
- **Don't roll your own auth** — use Keycloak, Cognito, Auth0, Okta

**OAuth2 vs DIY:**
- OAuth2/OIDC is the industry standard
- Self-hosting Keycloak or buying Auth0/Okta/Cognito beats building

**SAML vs OIDC:**
- OIDC: smaller, JSON, easier mobile/SPA
- SAML: enterprise mandates, legacy systems
- Many enterprises run both

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Session**: server state, instant revocation, simplest for first-party web.
- **JWT**: stateless, scales horizontally; revocation is hard — short expiry + blocklist.
- **OAuth2 / OIDC**: delegation + identity; use for third-party login, enterprise SSO, API auth.
- **SAML**: enterprise XML-based SSO; legacy + B2B; heavier than OIDC.
- **Short-lived access + rotatable refresh tokens** is the modern pattern.
- **PKCE mandatory** for mobile and SPA OAuth2 flows.
- **Never store JWT in `localStorage`** (XSS); HttpOnly cookie or in-memory.
- **Session: HttpOnly + Secure + SameSite cookies**; CSRF token for state changes.
- **Use a managed IdP** (Auth0, Okta, Keycloak, Cognito); don't roll your own.
- **Validate signature, `iss`, `aud`, `exp`** on every JWT; reject `alg: none`.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
**The four are different things**
- Session/JWT: token formats for authenticated requests
- OAuth2/OIDC/SAML: protocols for how to obtain tokens and delegate identity
- An OAuth2 flow can produce a JWT access token
- A session-based app can be authenticated via SAML SSO

**Decision framework**

*Session*
- First-party web app; server-rendered
- Need instant revocation
- Single domain
- Redis-backed for scale

*JWT raw*
- Service-to-service in your services
- Mobile/SPA to your API
- Stateless scaling
- Accept delayed revocation or implement `jti` blocklist

*OAuth2/OIDC*
- 'Login with Google/Microsoft/GitHub'
- Enterprise SSO with modern IdP
- Federated identity
- Microservice central auth
- Mobile with PKCE

*SAML*
- Enterprise B2B mandate
- Legacy systems
- ADFS, Azure AD SAML
- IdP-initiated flows

**Best practices condensed**
- Session: HttpOnly + Secure + SameSite + rotate on login
- JWT: short expiry + asymmetric signing + validate iss/aud/exp + don't `localStorage`
- OAuth2: Authorization Code + PKCE + state + validate ID token nonce
- SAML: sign assertions + validate cert + InResponseTo check + cert rotation plan

**2026 rule of thumb**
- First-party web -> session + cookies
- APIs / microservices -> OIDC JWT short-lived + refresh
- Enterprise SSO -> SAML or OIDC by customer
- Mobile -> OIDC + PKCE

**Avoid**
- Inventing your own token format
- Entire user object in JWT
- Long-lived JWT without revocation plan
- localStorage tokens
- Session without SameSite

**Mental model**
- Identity: who? (session, OIDC ID token, SAML assertion)
- Authorization: what can they do? (scopes, roles)
- Session format: cookie session ID, JWT, or opaque
- Pick each layer intentionally
